what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat a type of skin cancer called melanoma that has spread to other parts of the body or cannot be removed by surgery. It works by helping your immune system find and fight cancer cells more effectively. It contains two medicines — nivolumab and relatlimab — that work together to 'turn on' your immune system against cancer.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider through an IV (intravenous infusion) into a vein. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes. You will receive this treatment at a clinic or hospital. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely during and after your infusion.
dosing: The usual dose is nivolumab 480 mg combined with relatlimab 160 mg, given once every 4 weeks as an IV infusion. Your doctor may adjust your dose, delay treatment, or stop treatment depending on how your body responds or if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss or skip an appointment for your infusion, contact your doctor or care team as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to miss doses, as keeping up with your treatment schedule is important for the medicine to work as well as possible. Do not try to double up doses.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or hospital. You do not need to store it at home. If you are given any information about storage for home use, keep it in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Keep it out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you take before starting this medicine. Avoid taking corticosteroids or other medicines that suppress your immune system unless your doctor tells you to, as they may interfere with how this medicine works. Do not get live vaccines while on this treatment without talking to your doctor first. Avoid becoming pregnant, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby — use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: This medicine can cause your immune system to attack healthy organs, which can be serious or life-threatening. Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have any of these warning signs: new or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain (lungs); severe diarrhea, bloody stools, or stomach pain (intestines); yellowing of your skin or eyes, or dark urine (liver); feeling very tired, gaining or losing weight quickly, or feeling very hot or cold (hormones); severe headache, confusion, memory problems, or seizures (brain); rash, blistering, or peeling skin; muscle weakness or joint pain; changes in vision; signs of infection such as fever or chills; or any new or unusual symptoms. These side effects can happen weeks or months after your last dose.
when_it_works: Every patient responds differently to this medicine. Some people may notice benefits within weeks, while for others it may take longer. It is important to keep your appointments and continue treatment even if you do not feel different right away. Your doctor will use tests and scans to check how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. If you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant, tell your doctor right away. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children under 12 years of age have not been established. Older Adults: This medicine can be used in older adults, but talk to your doctor about any concerns. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how you are monitored during treatment.
